subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Decoy Effect
description: A micro-lesson that makes Decoy Effect usable.

hook.text: A magazine offered digital for $59 and print-plus-digital for $125. Few chose print. Then they added print-only at $125.

buildup.text: The print-only option was a decoy. Nobody chose it, but it made print-plus-digital look like a steal.

discovery.text: The decoy effect: adding an inferior option makes a target option look more attractive by comparison.

twist.text: Movie theatres use this with popcorn. The medium is priced near the large to push you toward the large.

climax.text: When three options appear and one seems pointless, it is there to nudge you. Spot the decoy and decide without it.

punchline.text: The worst option on the menu is there on purpose.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a decoy option?
options: To give customers a genuine low-cost alternative
To make a target option look better by comparison
To reduce the total number of choices

details.summary: The decoy effect occurs when adding an inferior third option changes the preference between two original options. The decoy is designed to be clearly worse than one target option but similar to it, making the target seem like the obvious superior choice.
details.whyItMatters: The decoy effect is widely used in pricing and product design. By adding a strategically inferior option, companies steer customers toward higher-margin products.
takeaways: An asymmetrically dominated option shifts preference toward the dominant alternative
The decoy does not need to sell; it just needs to make the target look better
Magazine subscriptions and pricing tiers commonly use decoy architecture

faq.question: What is the classic example of the decoy effect?
faq.answer: The Economist offered digital-only for 59 dollars, print-only for 125 dollars, and print-plus-digital for 125 dollars. The print-only option is a decoy that makes print-plus-digital look like an obvious bargain, since it costs the same but includes more.

faq.question: How does the decoy effect violate rational choice?
faq.answer: According to rational choice theory, adding an irrelevant option should not change the preference between existing options. The decoy effect shows that preferences are not stable but context-dependent, shifting based on what other options are visible.
